Express Home Staging
Introduction
Home staging isn't decorating: it's marketing. The goal isn't to please YOUR tastes, but to let the greatest number of buyers picture themselves — and to justify a better price, faster.
This guide gives you an express plan, room by room, doable in a weekend and without a big budget. Simple, high-impact moves.
Each chapter ends with a lined “My notes” page to check off your tasks, room by room.
Home staging isn't decorating: it's a sales strategy. Done well, it speeds up the sale and improves the offers — often for a few hundred dollars. This guide gets to the essentials, room by room.
The golden rule: the buyer must picture themselves. You depersonalize, you pare down, you bring in light.
The 3 principles that sell
Understanding the logic before moving a piece of furniture.
Understanding the logic before moving a piece of furniture.
Declutter: fewer objects = bigger, brighter rooms. It's move #1, free and the most profitable.
Depersonalize: put away family photos, mementos and strong tastes so the buyer imagines THEIR life here.
Neutralize and clean: subdued colours, a deep clean, neutral smells. A spotless house inspires confidence.
Remember: you don't decorate for yourself, you prepare a product for the market.

These three principles — declutter, depersonalize, bring in light — explain nearly all the effect of home staging. The buyer must be able to picture themselves: the less they see YOUR life, the more they imagine their own. And it costs mostly time, not money.
Emilie's tip
If you do only one thing: declutter massively. Clear out 30% of your things (boxes to the garage or storage). The effect on the perception of space is spectacular and free.
Exterior and entrance: the first impression
Winning the buyer over before they even step in.
Winning the buyer over before they even step in.
Façade: lawn mowed, hedges trimmed, driveway clear, bins hidden.
Front door: clean, a working handle, maybe a coat of paint.
Interior entrance: clear, bright, welcoming (a mirror, a plant).
The first impression plays out in a few seconds, from the sidewalk: it sets the tone for the whole visit.

The first impression plays out before the entrance: a neat façade, a clear driveway, a welcoming door. A tidy exterior promises a well-kept interior; a neglected one plants doubt from the sidewalk. A few hours of exterior cleanup pay off big.
Emilie's tip
Take a photo of your façade with your phone: the camera often reveals what the eye no longer sees (clutter, wear). Fix what the photo exposes.
Living areas and kitchen
Showcasing the spaces that sell.
Showcasing the spaces that sell.
Living room: clear the traffic paths, maximize the light, a few neutral touches.
Kitchen: counters almost empty, clean appliances, seals redone if needed.
Dining room: a simply set table to suggest conviviality.
Light everywhere: working bulbs, curtains open, a bright ambiance.
The kitchen and the light are two decisive factors: put your energy there first.

The living areas and the kitchen are the spaces that sell: clear the traffic paths, maximize the light, neutralize the décor and make the surfaces shine. A clean, pared-down kitchen, even a modest one, reassures far more than a cluttered one, even a high-end one.
Emilie's tip
Clear kitchen counters give an immediate impression of space and cleanliness. Put everything away except 1 or 2 decorative objects: it's one of the most effective moves there is.
Bedrooms, bathrooms and finishing touches
Tending to the intimate spaces and the details.
Tending to the intimate spaces and the details.
Bedrooms: neutral, tidy bedding, clear under the beds, decluttered closets (they look bigger).
Bathrooms: spotless, clean matching towels, clean seals and faucets, a neutral smell.
Finishing touches: fix what squeaks or sticks, air out, a pleasant temperature on visit day.
The details signal a well-kept house: they reassure the buyer and reduce their attempts to negotiate down.

Bedrooms and bathrooms sell through calm and cleanliness: neutral bedding, clear surfaces, clean seals, no marks. It's the details (smell, light, clear storage) that leave the impression of a healthy, well-kept house.
Emilie's tip
Partly empty your closets before visits: a half-full closet looks bigger and suggests “plenty of storage”. Buyers always open the doors.
